content:
I've been working my way through some Project Euler problems in Lean, often using a Lean iterator to represent a possibly infinite sequence of values (where I would simply use a list in a lazy language such as Haskell). For example:

-- 1. Find the sum of all the multiples of 3 or 5 below 1000.

def euler1 := (0 ... 1000).iter.filter (fun x => x % 3 == 0 || x % 5 == 0) |>.fold (· + ·) 0

-- 2. Find the sum of the even-valued values of the Fibonacci sequence below 4,000,000.

def all_fibs := Iter.repeat (fun (a, b) => (b, a + b)) (1, 1) |>.map (·.1)

def euler2 := all_fibs.takeWhile (· < 4_000_000) |>.filter (· % 2 == 0) |>.fold (· + ·) 0

On the whole Lean iterators work well, but I've found a few things to be inconvenient:

  1. Std.Iter is missing many of the useful functions that the library defines on List and Array, e.g. sum, product, max, maxOn, findIdx, idxOf, zipIdx, and so on. It's not hard to write them myself, but it would be nice if these were predefined.

  2. Std.Iter does not belong to the Functor, Applicative or Monad typeclasses. If it did, I could use e.g. <$> for mapping, or use an Iter in a do block.

  3. There is no implicit conversion from the range types (Std.Rco and so on) to Std.Iter, so I e.g. I have to write (0 ... 1000).iter.filter rather than just (0 ... 1000).filter in my first example above.

Regarding point (2), I tried to write my own instance declaration stating that Iter is a Functor, but found it was non-trivial because iterators are a bit complicated, and I didn't get it to work. As for point (3), I'm not sure whether this is even possible due to the way Lean searches for conversions.

Questions:

Concerning point (1) above, is the omission of these functions intentional? Would a pull request be welcome that adds many of these?

Concerning points (2) and (3), would it be technically feasible to fix these? If so, would these changes be welcome additions to the library?

Hi, author of the iterator library here. Thanks for the feedback! Some remarks:

  1. I agree, the iterator API is still lacking some functions that List and Array has. I think it is reasonable to add them. Sadly, I won't have the time to work on these in the next one or two months. If you are interested in making a PR against the standard library and willing to provide the verification API with it, I'd be happy to review and merge it. The library would profit from that. Perhaps request a review for a single operation first so that I can give you some early feedback.
  2. Yes, I think you won't be able to do that. it.map f has a different type than it has. That is deliberate; it allows the compiler to generate efficient code. The design is similar to Rust's iterator library in this regard. I'm not aware of a robust way to avoid these complicated types, but I'd be happy to learn about ways to avoid them while still generating efficient code.
  3. I think we should add more shortcuts such as Std.Roo.toArray. This should be quite trivial to do.

Hi Paul, thanks for your reply. Regarding (1), I think I should have some time in the coming weeks so OK, I'll try to look at the API and make a first pull request with just a single operation if possible. By there way is there any kind of paper or design document about your iterator implementation?

Regarding (2), it's a bit disappointing that iterators may never be able to implement Functor or related type classes, but it sounds like this was a deliberate tradeoff for purposes of efficiency. I hope to understand that a bit better once I've looked at the code more.

By the way I'll be at IJCAR in Lisbon this coming week - if you will too I'd be happy to meet up and discuss this more.

There is no paper, but the design is explained in the module docstring of Std.Data.Iterators and a reference manual chapter. Sadly, I'm not at IJCAR. Don't hesitate to ask if you have any questions about the library or design.

Adam Dingle said:

  • Std.Iter does not belong to the Functor, Applicative or Monad typeclasses. If it did, I could use e.g. <$> for mapping, or use an Iter in a do block.

I'd claim this is a problem with Functor; for similar reasons we can't have the operator on Finset or any other monad which has constraints on its parameter types. This has been discussed in depth in other threads.

That said, I admit that the iterators being so dependently typed makes proving things about them a bit annoying. I have plans to define "bundled iterators" that are of a fixed, simple type. Statement about the efficient, "unbundled" iterators will then be normalized to bundled iterators for verification purposes. I tend to make them noncomputable, for verification purposes only, but it is also conceivable to make them computable (but still less efficient).
